There's a site-wide faq (has anyone read it?) but it doesn't explain things like why the upvoat/downvoat limit is important. Or what you should be upvoating/dovwnvoating. We've been getting the same questions/threads in /v/introductions, /v/askvoat and /v/ideasforvoat over and over.

If we can't get a giant page that's impossible to miss maybe we can just use this post or something. I'll address a few here -

Upvoat/Downvoat limits - These are in place to prevent things like brigading and sock puppeting. Two huge problems at the other place. You want to lurk (a.k.a. not contribute) and then wander around upvoating and downvoating and you don't like that rule? Too bad. It makes this a much better place. On the plus side, the people who are contributing will continue to do all the work for you and you can continue to lurk. ;)

Upvoat/Downvoat usage - I'll post something I wrote elsewhere - "Please only downvoat stuff that doesn't contribute to the community you're in. You're in jokes? You pretty much don't need it. You're in news? Kindly downvoat everything that isn't actually part of a real discussion - puns, memes, etc. Feel butt hurt? Go call your mom and keep your downvoats to yourself. " So, please downvoat/upvoat based on the community you're in and keep in mind that it's not for telling someone you don't like their idea. That's what the comments are for. That's also why your voat limits are based on your contribution.

Submission Contribution Points (SCP) vs Comment Contribution Points (CCP) - This is like Link Karma and Comment Karma respectively at that other site. Once you hit 20 CCP, you get 100 upvoats per day. Downvotes are enabled when you reach 100 cumulative CCP. So, please don't spam subs asking people to upvoat your post, it does nothing.

This is beyond embarrassing. So many outlets are only eager to get the first/early scoop on something that appeals to their own core demographic. Sensationalism, pandering, infotainment, editorializing and agenda have muscled out so much real journalism. Outlets just want to throw up things as quickly as they can which their particular readership will lap up, rather than investigate and fact check. People can even convince themselves they are well read worldly because you can cherry pick several sources that share your preferred perspective and you assume there's been some due diligence.

But for those that do pay attention and not forget things literally the day after they happen, this just confirms that "news" outlets are PURE CRAP, and deserve to be ridiculed constantly.

Journalist here!

I'm going to explain why this happened: basically why this occurred was a high profile person or celebrity made a false statement that gave the impression that this was a truthful story; it happens all the time unfortunately. We see it when ANYONE with authority or notoriety makes a claim - its automatically believed by the press.

The organization I'm with make a point to take everything we are told with a grain of salt and fact check to the best of our ability. We don't report personal statements as fact, only as opinion or we use terms like "allegedly."

We do "rebranding" like everyone else to fill up content, but we tend to shy away from things we can't prove or are not on video. Most internet media doesn't even bother with this and the main stream media only cares if they are caught.

To reiterate, I am only looking for personal accounts and not generalizations on how it happened.
I am doing research on the 2008 financial crisis and the impact that it had for people in the United States. I am looking for personal accounts on how it affected you or someone you are close with.

Just before the crisis, the housing market was booming. Many realtors, my company included, were in the process of constructing large subdivisions with $500,000 - $1,000,000 houses on them. They were selling like hotcakes, you just couldn't build em fast enough to keep up.

Market Crash.

Until only very recently, those subdivisions remained half-built, or completely empty, and the ones which had been finished building got it the worst, since they now had to pay taxes on hundreds of very expensive lots with very expensive houses on them, and no one was buying.

I was in college at the time and graduated in 2010. I moved a few times afterward and had no issues finding work in OH, TX and CO. I used the internet, phone calls and applying in person to land jobs, and while I'd like to be making more money (who wouldn't?) I'm living alone and supporting myself in a place I love.

I think the recession was much harder on people who had become accustomed to a certain lifestyle before 2008 and were forced to adjust.

I was working in the Automotive industry. 2005-2007 were very good years, and many fellow Mechanics will recall making around 6 figures during this time. 2008 was a completely different story. I remember going to work some days and sitting around for 8 hours. Sometimes I would get one job or two. Managers and dispatchers were accused of favoratism because some mechanics were getting more work than others. It was an all around miserable time to work in the industry.

Shops started closing slowly and continue to close 'til this day. The automotive industry never recovered. People just dont service or maintenance their vehicles like they used to. They drive them until they break down and are forced to spend.

I left the industry two years ago and I'm now making salary. I still hear from old friends about the extremely competitive nature of shops, because there is still not enough work.

I was in the Army at the time, and I had to watch people's financial problems destroy the careers they had worked so long for. If their finances suffered, they lost a home to the mortgage crisis, or had outstanding debt, then they would lose their security clearance and be forced out or made to change professions. It also affected people trying to get in to the military out of desperation for not finding a job, and realizing they weren't eligible for certain jobs because of their debt from not having a job.

[I had to watch people's financial problems destroy the careers they had worked so long for.]

Could you elaborate a little more on this for me? What type of financial problems were they having and more specifically what do you believe were the causes of those financial problems as it relates to the 08 crisis.

I have not come across the issue of not being able to get into the military. How many of these people did you personally know and what what the official reason MEPS gave them? If you would be able to get documentation on that, it would help a lot.

Well it wasn't meps. I was a recruiter from 2008-2011 after spending the majority of my career in the special ops community. People that we identified with financial issues never even made it to meps, or were put into jobs that didn't require a clearance. The security clearances used to adjudicate certain financial issues if you were actively trying to fix them, but as they became more common, and the deployments began slowing down, they became stricter. I watched guys, one in particular who had been in the Reserves for 23 years, and was a cop on the civilian side, lose two homes to foreclosure during the crisis. They had bought before the bubble as an investment property in 2005. By the time he came back from his second deployment in the middle of the crisis, he was already flagged for his clearance being suspended. When the dust settled and the houses were gone, his adjudicate denied because there was no longer a need to push clearances through because of a troop shortage. So he was told to reclass to a non clearance or get out. And in the special ops community, even the jobs that don't typically require a clearance still requires one because of their positions.

Graduated college in 2008, spent the last 7 years taking any job I could get, basically -- waiting tables, working in a call center, fixing TVs, etc. It's been really horrible actually, and I wish I never spent the money on college. It has been probably the biggest mistake of my life so far because I owe like $35k and it hasn't helped me in any of my bullshit jobs I've been able to get.

I sort of feel duped, because left to my own devices, I would not have gone to college right out of highschool because I didn't have a fuckin clue what I wanted to study or what I'd could excel at/ enjoy professionally one day, but everyone from my parents (who never went to college themselves and were simply feeding off the general buzz at the time), to my teachers, to politicians on television made the case that you either go to college or become a failure in life. If I'd had a second to think about it, I could probably have made more out of college, but as a 17 year-old high school senior, asking me what I wanted to study in college was basically like asking a kid what they want to have for dinner: "Candy! Ice Cream!". So I picked some bullshit Liberal Arts degree and I have no practical profitable skills.

In 2008 I was a college student majoring in economics. I think I was in macroeconomic analysis the semester when the shit hit the fan. Every other class the professor would come in waving a newspaper going, "I was going to teach this thing, but fuck it, this thing doesn't apply anymore. The apocalypse is here. Lets study that instead."

Best economics class ever.

I was working as a structural engineer in SE Michigan at the time. My wife and I got married in late 2008 and I was laid off two weeks after I returned from my honeymoon. We ended up having to move to Indianapolis so she could have a secure job while I tried to find a new position. I was out of work for a total of 10 months. Since then we have moved to Central Ohio and are only now getting things back on track. 2014 was the first year of our marriage that we both worked all 12 months of the year. My spouse and I both have STEM degrees with solid work histories and even that was not enough to protect us from the actions of the banks.
Lost my retirement savings and all of my dreams for the good life. Have a pension and am not starving, but the dreams are gone.

My father used to work at a soda can manufacturing plant. The company he worked for printed many big names: Monster, Dr.Pepper, Minute Maid, etc... The factory he worked at was an overflow plant meaning that the work they did was primarily to handle volume that "overflowed" when other factories were running at or near maximum capacity. He was responsible for a large portion of the quality control on several of the production lines. His job entailed approving prints before, during and after production as well as maintaining and indexing all of the calibrations and resources necessary for exactly recreating each print job. This job is what he considers to be the pinnacle of his career. He loved the work, was thought very highly of, and made an excellent salary.

The economy tanked, and beverage manufactures scaled back production. In a matter of just a couple months the steady streams of work dried up to a trickle at best until they ceased production entirely and laid off, or offered positions at other plants to all the employees. My parents weren't in a position to move across the country so that was that. He then tried to run his own small business which failed, and he was unemployed for over a year before he took a dead end job making $11.50/hr. My father is almost 60 years old and at this point has very little hope of ever getting another position like he held before.
